pages.h1: Insurance support or self-pay GLP-1 telehealth?
intro: Insurance support and insurance coverage are different. A telehealth company can check benefits, help with paperwork, or submit a prior authorization, but the plan still controls formulary rules, approval, and out-of-pocket cost. Self-pay programs trade that uncertainty for a published cash price, often with a commitment or compounded-drug limitation.

Found is the insurance-support winner in this set because it publishes a free insurance check and carrier support. yourEra and Trimi are clearer self-pay comparators. Shed describes both insurance and cash-pay paths, but its published starting price can change with medication and dose.
None of these commercial paths establishes medical eligibility. Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, and plan coverage for a drug or indication can change.
pros: Separates navigation help from actual coverage
Shows a self-pay fallback beside insurance-support options
Keeps plan-specific and eligibility caveats visible

intro: Trimi and Shed make different commercial promises visible. Trimi's checked homepage leads with a compact flat-price bundle: compounded semaglutide at $99 per month and compounded tirzepatide at $125 per month on annual plans, with the same price at every dose. The page says one membership covers the medication, clinician visits, ongoing check-ins, and free shipping. Shed's product page presents a broader catalog and payment-path story, including insurance or cash-pay wording, branded and compounded options, and a pricing card that lists medication, supplies, member support, and shipping. Its price display is not one clean number. The checked page shows 'Starting at $149/month +' in one section, $199 per month in a later pricing card, and site banners advertising compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide at other figures. Shed's terms add another relevant layer by identifying $199 semaglutide and $299 tirzepatide as the current standard monthly rates after the minimum term for multi-month subscriptions. This page does not select the most favorable number. It records each context and tells the reader to verify the selected product, term, and cart before payment.

The contract evidence reverses the visibility pattern. Trimi's homepage clearly labels the lowest prices as annual-plan rates but does not publish the annual billing schedule, early-cancellation process, cutoff, or general refund calculation in the checked homepage content. That makes its bundle easy to understand at the headline level and incomplete at the commitment level. Shed's terms are much more explicit. They say medication programs renew automatically every 28 days or monthly depending on the program, impose a two-full-month minimum, and require cancellation at least 72 hours before the next billing date or scheduled shipment for the request to affect that cycle. General subscription fees are described as non-refundable once charged. The multi-month section says cancellation is available after the minimum term through the portal, an email cancellation link, or support; shipped cycles are treated as used; cancellation does not automatically trigger a refund; and an eligible amount for unfulfilled cycles may be calculated after used months are repriced at the applicable month-to-month rate. The terms also describe narrower exceptions. Those rules are commercially useful because they answer what happens after checkout. They do not prove that Shed's total is lower, that every plan uses the same cadence, or that a particular refund request will be approved.

Gala GLP-1 and Wellorithm appear only as benchmark context. Gala's checked page presents compounded GLP-1/GIP at $179 per month and labels the calculation as a yearly subscription plan; it also states that compounded GLP-1 is not FDA-approved. Wellorithm's checked page presents compounded semaglutide starting at $147 and compounded tirzepatide starting at $249, says no insurance is required, and includes free-shipping language. Neither benchmark receives ownership of this page, and neither price is treated as a quote for another plan. The Trimi-versus-Shed decision is narrower: a compact annual-plan bundle versus a multi-product offer backed by more visible subscription terms. Audit that obligation on a billing calendar: mark the enrollment timestamp, installment dates, renewal anniversary, shipment cycles, dispatch notices, prepaid balance, repricing formula, cancellation cutoff, submission proof, and acknowledgment email. Save the selected SKU, cart, invoice, courier identifier, card descriptor, and plan-length disclosure together. This catches timing exposure that an amortized monthly headline hides. There is no medical winner. Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, and FDA says they are not reviewed before marketing for safety, effectiveness, or quality. FDA recommends obtaining a prescription and using a state-licensed pharmacy. A licensed provider decides whether to prescribe. This four-row comparison looks for two narrow kinds of public evidence: clinician-review visibility and shipping-process visibility. HealthRX's accepted row states independent physician file review within 24 hours and free overnight shipping. AgelessRx states free discreet shipping in 3–5 business days and mentions licensed U.S. clinician review without a review duration in the accepted row. Wellorithm states free direct-to-door shipping while dispatch and delivery timing are not stated. Enhance.MD states that medication is shipped to the door and describes a 12-week cadence, but no delivery window. Those statements do not share one starting event, so they are not combined into an intake-to-door race.

Read every row as an event map. Intake may precede clinician review; a decision may precede prescription routing; pharmacy processing may precede carrier handoff; delivery follows the carrier stage. A published clock belongs only in the stage its wording supports. For AgelessRx, Wellorithm, and Enhance.MD, clinician-review timing is Not stated in the accepted rows. For Wellorithm, dispatch and delivery timing are Not stated. For Enhance.MD, the delivery window is Not stated. Missing clocks stay visible because replacing them with estimates would create a speed claim that the source record does not support. Record the stated trigger beside every duration. If the trigger is absent, mark it Not stated as well; a numerical band without a defined starting event cannot be aligned confidently with another provider's band. Keep cadence, processing, dispatch, transit, and arrival in separate columns. That structure prevents a refill interval from masquerading as delivery time and prevents a shipping phrase from becoming a claim about clinician review.

The frozen scores remain unchanged. HealthRX carries the highest accepted shipping-transparency and medical-oversight scores in this set, but that is an evidence finding, not a statement about clinical quality, medical suitability, prescription approval, guaranteed speed, safety, or outcomes. AgelessRx supplies a stated delivery band. Wellorithm makes free direct-to-door shipping visible without an elapsed window. Enhance.MD makes home shipping and a cadence visible without a carrier window. Each pattern tells a shopper which operational questions remain. Prices and program fields were checked through July 23, 2026 and can change. Verify current offers and enrollment terms directly.
